content: This case involved a request for the dissolution of a hereditary communion regarding several buildings and lands. The court operated within the framework of Articles 1113 and 784 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which govern the division of common property. The core interpretive problem was determining the minimum evidentiary threshold required to prove the ownership of the assets and the completeness of the parties involved. The court ruled that the claim was radically inadmissible because the plaintiff failed to produce certified registry results from the "Conservatoria" or a twenty-year history of property titles. The principle applied is that the right to divide an estate cannot be established solely through the parties' allegations or simple technical reports; instead, rigorous documentation of the property’s legal status and the identification of all necessary parties (such as creditors or co-owners) is a non-negotiable prerequisite for the action.
